name: Patrice Lumumba
role: First prime minister of the Republic of the Congo (June-September 1960); leader of the Congolese National Movement
summary: Congolese nationalist and pan-Africanist who led the MNC to independence in 1960 and opposed colonial discrimination and exploitation. He favoured a unitary state, rejected Katanga's secession, practised positive neutrality in the cold war and favoured state-led development. In the crisis he appealed to the UN and the Soviet Union and defended Parliament's authority until his arrest and killing.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Lumumba kept the national army in place and appointed its Congolese commander and chief of staff in July 1960.

civilizational-union.rationale: Lumumba signed a plan for a federal Union of African States open to every African state and territory.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Rejected delay or transition: 'There can be no compromise between freedom and slavery', whatever positive aspects of the colonial system.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Condemned colonial rule as forced labour, seizure of land and exploitation, and demanded its abolition.

common-currency.rationale: Lumumba signed the Ghana–Congo agreement proposing that a federal government issue a common currency for the African states in the union.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Argued a government may be dismissed only when it loses the people's trust and Parliament's confidence, and proposed a referendum to let the people choose their leaders.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: As prime minister he Africanised the army command, appointing Congolese officers to senior posts previously held by Belgians.

defeat-communism.rationale: In his Washington press exchange (pp. 304–305), Lumumba treated the Soviet Union on the same footing as other countries and said positive neutrality allowed dealings with any state that respected Congo’s independence.

direct-action.rationale: Lumumba sought to settle the September 1960 dispute over who governed through Parliament, relying on its votes and continuing to exercise the premiership with its backing.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Proposed in November 1960 a referendum on a presidential regime followed by direct election of the President.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Asked in February 1960 about permitting marriages between Black and white people (pp. 182–183), Lumumba rejected drawing racial boundaries around whom people could love.

dominated-front.rationale: Called on African states to form a united resistance front against imperialist powers while rejecting entry into cold-war blocs.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: In August 1960 Lumumba instituted a six-month military regime in which military and popular tribunals would take over from the civilian courts.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: In his 7 August telegram to the Security Council, Lumumba proposed a UN observer group specifically charged with enforcing the Council’s decisions requiring Belgium to withdraw troops from the Congo, including Katanga.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Lumumba demanded an end to laws that discriminated by race and invoked the Universal Declaration as a guarantee for every person. In his earlier book he challenged rules that kept qualified Congolese below less-qualified Europeans in the public service.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Sought a Congolese nation of many tribes in which Europeans who stayed would also share; fought tribalism as a poison.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: In August 1960 Lumumba attempted to airlift army units to Kasai to prevent the province’s attempted secession.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: In his 1 August telegram to the Security Council and his opening speech at the All-African Conference, Lumumba said that Belgium and other imperial powers were backing secession to break up the Congo and regain control of its resources.

former-empire-equal-treatment.rationale: In the February Round Table discussion (pp. 178–179), Lumumba granted Belgium a prior moral claim arising from its previous role in the Congo while affirming that the independent Congo could call on other countries too.

free-public-college.rationale: In his December 1958 post-Accra address (pp. 62–64), Lumumba proposed free and compulsory education at all levels, along with state scholarships.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Pledged to eradicate all discrimination whatever its origin and condemned whites-only shops, restaurants and cinemas.

government-encourage-intercultural-conta.rationale: Opening the All-African Conference, Lumumba put government-supported cultural exchanges on the agenda as a way to break down barriers inherited from colonial rule.

head-of-state-dissolves-parliament.rationale: After Kasa-Vubu suspended Parliament, Lumumba wrote to the UN General Assembly president that the head of state had no right under the parliamentary system to suspend its supreme organ.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: At the February Round Table (pp. 178–179), Lumumba said political independence would mean nothing unless accompanied by economic development aimed at meeting people’s needs and improving their living conditions.

keep-colonial-borders.rationale: Lumumba attempted to send troops to Kasai when its southern part threatened to join the secession of Katanga, seeking to hold the inherited territory together.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Honoured fighters who died for independence: 'Eternal glory to the fighters for national liberation'.

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: Lumumba attempted to move Congolese troops to Kasai to prevent an internal secession and preserve the Congolese state’s authority over the region.

national-resource-control.rationale: At the February Round Table (pp. 174–175), Lumumba described mineral and hydroelectric resources as a common Congolese patrimony and assigned control over prospecting rights and regulation to the central government.

night-watchman-state.rationale: As prime minister he signed a contract to organise development of minerals and hydroelectric power, putting the government in an economic development role.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: In December 1958 (pp. 62–63), Lumumba called on Congolese of all religions to unite in one political front. In August 1960 (pp. 314–315) he rejected confessional control of government.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: In August 1960, Lumumba declared that African countries should no longer permit former occupying powers to station armed forces at bases such as Kamina and Kitona.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Called Parliament 'the only sovereign body in the country' and 'the country's supreme organ', over the head of state.

party-controls-media.rationale: Lumumba’s government required newspapers to apply for permission to publish and issued an ordinance barring Europe-Magazine. Lumumba also decreed the creation of a state news agency to replace Belga’s local service.

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: At the April 1959 Présence Africaine meeting (pp. 79–80), Lumumba condemned political violence and argued that political goals could be achieved by peaceful means. He reaffirmed the movement’s nonviolent policy at his July 1960 New York press conference (pp. 286–287).

pool-sovereignty.rationale: On 8 August 1960 Lumumba signed an agreement with Nkrumah for a federal union with a parliament and shared authority over foreign affairs, defence, currency and economic planning, subject to approval in both countries.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Aimed to revive Africa's cultural, philosophical, social and moral values.

public-ownership.rationale: Asked about state ownership of railway and power companies in February 1960 (p. 172), Lumumba said his programme did not call for nationalisation and that existing large companies would continue to operate.

racial-franchise.rationale: Called the colonial equal-seats arrangement for the European minority and African majority anti-democratic; sought a democratic state with equality and no discrimination.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Denounced racially segregated housing, cinemas, restaurants and transport and demanded immediate elimination of racial discrimination and colonial-era unjust laws.

regional-resource-ownership.rationale: At the February Round Table (pp. 174–175), Lumumba rejected provincial ownership of mining and hydroelectric resources and held that these belonged to the entire country under central regulation.

remove-other-ethnic-groups-from-country.rationale: At the February 1960 Round Table (pp. 164–166), Lumumba rejected expelling European residents and invited them to remain and take part in Congolese society.

right-to-secede.rationale: Lumumba attempted to send Congolese troops to Kasai in August 1960 to stop its attempted secession.

separate-church-state.rationale: In August 1960 (pp. 314–315), Lumumba called for separation of church and state, promised that the government would stay out of church affairs, and rejected church intervention in government affairs.

state-directs-investment.rationale: In July 1960 Lumumba signed an agreement with CIMCO that directed development toward mining, oil, gas and hydroelectric power. The agreement required approval by the Congolese legislature.

state-harmful.rationale: Lumumba exercised the authority of the national government as prime minister and convened its Council of Ministers to contest his dismissal in September 1960.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Opening the All-African Conference in August 1960, Lumumba rejected alignment with either Cold War bloc and said the Congo would deal with countries according to their conduct toward Africa.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: In August 1960 (pp. 314–315), Lumumba pledged that his government would leave the affairs of churches to the churches themselves.

women-organise-apart-from-men.rationale: At the February Round Table meeting (p. 174), Lumumba described establishing the Union of Democratic Women of the Congo to organise women politically across the country.

women-suffrage.rationale: In his February 1960 Brussels address (pp. 168–169), Lumumba demanded equal political rights for women and men and called for both to vote from age eighteen.

notes: The December 1958–September 1960 speeches, debates and interviews were searched across economic development, land, work and wages, government, elections, constitutional powers, civil liberties, society, religious institutions, culture, international relations and anti-colonial methods. Technology and ecology searches covered technical education, broadcasting, mineral and hydroelectric development and land, with other topics unsupported. Also checked the contemporary UN and US records, the July development agreement, the August press record, and the original French excerpt from Le Congo, terre d’avenir est-il menacé ? (Conclusion, part 1). Wikipedia references are retained for the signed history of the previous pass.
